claim: PP2A is a major and the most abundant serine/threonine phosphatase in mammalian cells.
source: Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a major and the most abundant serine/threonine phosphatase in mammalian cells and dephosphorylates ~half cellular proteins (Arnold and Sears, 2008; Virshup, 2000; Wlodarchak and Xing, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arnold and Sears, 2008; Virshup, 2000; Wlodarchak and Xing, 2016

claim: PP2A dephosphorylates approximately half of cellular proteins.
source: Protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) is a major and the most abundant serine/threonine phosphatase in mammalian cells and dephosphorylates ~half cellular proteins (Arnold and Sears, 2008; Virshup, 2000; Wlodarchak and Xing, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Arnold and Sears, 2008; Virshup, 2000; Wlodarchak and Xing, 2016

claim: PP2A holoenzymes consist of a dimeric core enzyme formed by the scaffolding A and catalytic C subunits and a diverse set of regulatory B subunits.
source: The cellular functions of PP2A rely on the formation of structurally distinct diverse heterotrimeric holoenzymes; each consists of a dimeric core enzyme formed by the scaffolding A and catalytic C (C or PP2Ac) subunits and a diverse set of regulatory B subunits.
evidence: Established structural knowledge about PP2A holoenzyme composition

claim: PP2A regulatory subunits belong to four major families: B/B55/PR55, B′/B56/PR61, B″/PR72, and B⁗/Striatin.
source: The regulatory subunits belong to four major families (B/B55/PR55, B′/B56/PR61, B″/PR72, and B⁗/Striatin), and dictate specific substrate recognition.
evidence: Established classification of PP2A regulatory subunits

claim: PP2A holoenzymes recognize substrates by binding to short linear motifs (SLiMs) in substrates.
source: Recent studies arrive at a merging theme that PP2A holoenzymes recognize substrates by binding to short linear motifs (SLiMs) in substrates (Hertz et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Wu et al., 2017a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hertz et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Wu et al., 2017a

claim: PP2A holoenzymes are highly regulated by carboxymethylation of the PP2Ac tail.
source: PP2A holoenzymes are highly regulated by carboxymethylation of the PP2Ac tail, which is reversibly controlled by PP2A-specific leucine carboxyl methyltransferase (LCMT-1) (De Baere et al., 1999; Lee and Stock, 1993) and methylesterase (PME-1) (Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Baere et al., 1999; Lee and Stock, 1993; Lee et al., 1996

claim: PP2Ac tail carboxymethylation is reversibly controlled by LCMT-1 and PME-1.
source: PP2A holoenzymes are highly regulated by carboxymethylation of the PP2Ac tail, which is reversibly controlled by PP2A-specific leucine carboxyl methyltransferase (LCMT-1) (De Baere et al., 1999; Lee and Stock, 1993) and methylesterase (PME-1) (Lee et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to De Baere et al., 1999; Lee and Stock, 1993; Lee et al., 1996

claim: Dysregulation of PP2A holoenzymes or alteration of holoenzyme functions causes many human diseases, including cancer, heart diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders.
source: Dysregulation of PP2A holoenzymes or alteration of holoenzyme functions causes many human diseases, including cancer, heart diseases, and neurodegenerative disorders (Janssens et al., 2005; Sontag et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to Janssens et al., 2005; Sontag et al., 2004

claim: LCMT-1 is essential for cell survival.
source: Consistently, LCMT-1 is essential for cell survival (Lee and Pallas, 2007), and the deletion of PME-1 in mice is perinatally lethal (Ortega-Gutiérrez et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lee and Pallas, 2007

claim: The deletion of PME-1 in mice is perinatally lethal.
source: Consistently, LCMT-1 is essential for cell survival (Lee and Pallas, 2007), and the deletion of PME-1 in mice is perinatally lethal (Ortega-Gutiérrez et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ortega-Gutiérrez et al., 2008

claim: LCMT-1 and PME-1 activity on the PP2Ac tail relies on binding to the phosphatase active site.
source: Their activity on the PP2Ac tail, 'TPDYFL' relies on binding to the phosphatase active site, which induces significant changes in LCMT-1 to accommodate the tail (Stanevich et al., 2011) and global conformational changes in PME-1 to create the substrate-binding pocket and the active configuration of the catalytic triads (Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stanevich et al., 2011 and Xing et al., 2008

claim: Binding to the phosphatase active site induces significant changes in LCMT-1 to accommodate the PP2Ac tail.
source: Their activity on the PP2Ac tail, 'TPDYFL' relies on binding to the phosphatase active site, which induces significant changes in LCMT-1 to accommodate the tail (Stanevich et al., 2011) and global conformational changes in PME-1 to create the substrate-binding pocket and the active configuration of the catalytic triads (Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stanevich et al., 2011

claim: Binding to the phosphatase active site induces global conformational changes in PME-1 to create the substrate-binding pocket and the active configuration of the catalytic triads.
source: Their activity on the PP2Ac tail, 'TPDYFL' relies on binding to the phosphatase active site, which induces significant changes in LCMT-1 to accommodate the tail (Stanevich et al., 2011) and global conformational changes in PME-1 to create the substrate-binding pocket and the active configuration of the catalytic triads (Xing et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xing et al., 2008

claim: LCMT-1 activity is enhanced by the activation of PP2Ac and its association with the A-subunit.
source: The LCMT-1 activity is enhanced by the activation of PP2Ac and its association with the A-subunit and is thus highly selective toward the active core enzyme, (Stanevich et al., 2011; Stanevich et al., 2014), ensuring that PP2A is either in latent, inactive or in active substrate-specific forms.
evidence: Supported by citations to Stanevich et al., 2011; Stanevich et al., 2014

claim: LCMT-1 is highly selective toward the active core enzyme.
source: The LCMT-1 activity is enhanced by the activation of PP2Ac and its association with the A-subunit and is thus highly selective toward the active core enzyme, (Stanevich et al., 2011; Stanevich et al., 2014), ensuring that PP2A is either in latent, inactive or in active substrate-specific forms.
evidence: Supported by citations to Stanevich et al., 2011; Stanevich et al., 2014

claim: PP2A holoenzymes are predominately methylated in cells.
source: PP2A holoenzymes are predominately methylated in cells (Tolstykh et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2000; Yu et al., 2001), suggesting that PME-1 might not directly demethylate holoenzymes.
evidence: Supported by citations to Tolstykh et al., 2000; Wu et al., 2000; Yu et al., 2001

claim: PP2A holoenzymes are thermodynamically the most stable form of PP2A and have nanomolar intersubunit binding affinities.
source: Holoenzymes are also thermaldynamically the most stable form of PP2A and have nanomolar intersubunit binding affinities (Chen et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chen et al., 2007

claim: PP2A interacts with dynamic regulatory proteins with micromolar binding affinities, such as LCMT-1, PME-1, TIPRL, and α4.
source: In contrast, PP2A interacts with dynamic regulatory proteins with micromolar binding affinities, such as LCMT-1, PME-1, TIPRL (TOR signaling pathway regulator-like), and α4.
evidence: Established knowledge about PP2A binding affinities with regulatory proteins

claim: Structural overlay of PP2A holoenzymes and the PP2A core enzyme–PME-1 complex indicates that PP2A regulatory subunits would hinder PME-1 binding and prevent it from acting on holoenzymes.
source: Structural overlay of PP2A holoenzymes (Wlodarchak et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2006) and the PP2A core enzyme–PME-1 complex (Xing et al., 2008) indicates that PP2A regulatory subunits would hinder PME-1 binding and prevent it from acting on holoenzymes (Figure 1a).
evidence: Based on structural comparison and inference from crystal structures cited (Wlodarchak et al., 2013; Xu et al., 2008; Xu et al., 2006; Xing et al., 2008) and shown in Figure 1a

claim: TIPRL/α4 readily disassemble unmethylated PP2A holoenzymes by perturbing the phosphatase active site and inducing global conformational changes in PP2Ac.
source: TIPRL/α4 readily disassemble unmethylated PP2A holoenzymes by perturbing the phosphatase active site and inducing global conformational changes in PP2Ac (Jiang et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017b).
evidence: Supported by citations to Jiang et al., 2013; Wu et al., 2017b

claim: PP2A holoenzymes were found to be cofractionated with PME-1 in tissue extracts.
source: Furthermore, PP2A holoenzymes were found to be cofractionated with PME-1 in tissue extracts (Longin et al., 2004; Tolstykh et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Longin et al., 2004; Tolstykh et al., 2000

claim: Robust PP2A demethylation was detected after mammalian cells were lysed.
source: Robust PP2A demethylation was detected after the mammalian cells were lysed (Yabe et al., 2018), suggesting that PP2A holoenzymes might be demethylated upon their spatial separation from PME-1 was disrupted.
evidence: Supported by citation to Yabe et al., 2018

claim: PME-1 readily demethylates different families of PP2A holoenzymes in vitro.
source: Here, we showed that PME-1 readily demethylates different families of PP2A holoenzymes and blocks substrate recognition in vitro.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1e

claim: PME-1 blocks substrate recognition by PP2A holoenzymes in vitro.
source: Here, we showed that PME-1 readily demethylates different families of PP2A holoenzymes and blocks substrate recognition in vitro.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: PME-1 disordered regions, including a substrate-mimicking motif, tether to the B56 regulatory subunit at remote sites.
source: The high-resolution cryoelectron microscopy structure of a PP2A-B56 holoenzyme–PME-1 complex reveals that PME-1 disordered regions, including a substrate-mimicking motif, tether to the B56 regulatory subunit at remote sites.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: PME-1 disordered regions occupy the holoenzyme substrate-binding groove.
source: They occupy the holoenzyme substrate-binding groove and allow large structural shifts in both holoenzyme and PME-1 to enable multipartite contacts at structured cores to activate the methylesterase.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: PME-1 binding allows large structural shifts in both holoenzyme and PME-1 to enable multipartite contacts at structured cores to activate the methylesterase.
source: They occupy the holoenzyme substrate-binding groove and allow large structural shifts in both holoenzyme and PME-1 to enable multipartite contacts at structured cores to activate the methylesterase.
evidence: Supported by cryo-EM structural data shown in Figures 3 and 4

claim: B56 interface mutations selectively block PME-1 activity toward PP2A-B56 holoenzymes.
source: B56 interface mutations selectively block PME-1 activity toward PP2A-B56 holoenzymes and affect the methylation of a fraction of total cellular PP2A.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5a and Figure 5—figure supplement 1

claim: B56 interface mutations affect the methylation of a fraction of total cellular PP2A.
source: B56 interface mutations selectively block PME-1 activity toward PP2A-B56 holoenzymes and affect the methylation of a fraction of total cellular PP2A.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6a, b

claim: B56 interface mutations allow uncovering B56-specific PME-1 functions in p53 signaling.
source: The B56 interface mutations allow us to uncover B56-specific PME-1 functions in p53 signaling.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6

claim: PME-1 comigrates stoichiometrically with the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme over gel filtration chromatography.
source: Contradictory to this structural prediction, PME-1 comigrates stoichiometrically with the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme over gel filtration chromatography (Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1b and Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: B56γ1 represents the conserved common core in B56 subunits.
source: B56γ1 represents the conserved common core in B56 subunits (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by domain structure analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: PME-1 comigrates stoichiometrically with the PP2A-B56ε holoenzyme.
source: Consistent with this notion, we also observed stoichiometric comigration of PME-1 and the PP2A-B56ε holoenzyme (Figure 1—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1c

claim: PME-1 interacts with B56 holoenzymes and induces a more open holoenzyme conformation.
source: These data showed that that PME-1 interacts with B56 holoenzymes and induces a more open holoenzyme conformation.
evidence: Supported by FRET data shown in Figure 1c

claim: PME-1-mRuby readily interacts with PP2Ac and multiple HA-tagged regulatory subunits in the B56 family (B56β, B56γ1, B56γ3, and B56δ) in mammalian cell lysates.
source: PME-1-mRuby readily interacts with PP2Ac and multiple HA-tagged regulatory subunits in the B56 family, B56β, B56γ1, B56γ3, and B56δ (Figure 1d), supporting the earlier notion that PME-1 interacts with the common core in B56 subunits.
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1d

claim: B56δ interacts with a much higher ratio of PP2Ac over PME-1 compared to other B56 family members.
source: Compared to other B56 family members, B56δ interacts with a much higher ratio of PP2Ac over PME-1 (Figure 1d), suggesting that the interaction between PME-1 and the PP2A-B56δ holoenzyme might be reduced by other structural elements unique to B56δ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1d and inference from domain structure in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: A much lower stoichiometric amount of PME-1 comigrates with the PP2A-B56δ holoenzyme over gel filtration chromatography.
source: Consistently, a much lower stoichiometric amount of PME-1 comigrates with the PP2A-B56δ holoenzyme over gel filtration chromatography (Figure 1—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1d

claim: The recombinant B56δ associates with PP2Ac at a much higher level compared to other B56 subunits.
source: The recombinant B56δ associates with PP2Ac at a much higher level compared to other B56 subunits (Figure 1d).
evidence: Supported by co-IP data shown in Figure 1d

claim: The resistance of the PP2A-B56δ holoenzyme to PME-1 likely renders it less prone to demethylation and TIPRL/α4-mediated holoenzyme disassembly.
source: The resistance of this holoenzyme to PME-1 likely renders it less prone to demethylation and TIPRL/α4-mediated holoenzyme disassembly.
evidence: Inference based on the observed reduced PME-1 interaction with B56δ holoenzyme

claim: PME-1 catalyzes demethylation of methylated core enzyme and holoenzymes in vitro.
source: After incubation with PME-1, the methylation level of all three holoenzymes decreases significantly, comparable to that of the core enzyme (Figure 1e).
evidence: Supported by demethylation assay data shown in Figure 1e

claim: PME-1-PP2A holoenzyme interactions enable all sequential events needed for PME-1 activation, allowing PME-1 to demethylate PP2A holoenzymes directly.
source: Our results suggest that PME-1-PP2A holoenzyme interactions enable all sequential events needed for PME-1 activation, allowing PME-1 to demethylate PP2A holoenzymes directly.
evidence: Inference based on demethylation data shown in Figure 1e

claim: PME-1 has two ~40-residue disordered regions at the N-terminus and the internal loop.
source: PME-1 has two ~40-residue disordered regions at the N-terminus and the internal loop (Figure 2a).
evidence: Structural knowledge shown in Figure 2a

claim: The PME-1 internal loop harbors a SLiM (251VEGIIEE258E) highly similar to B56 substrates that interact with the conserved B56 common core via a signature motif 'LxxIxE'.
source: The latter harbors a SLiM (251VEGIIEE258E) highly similar to B56 substrates that interact with the conserved B56 common core via a signature motif 'LxxIxE' (Hertz et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Wu et al., 2017a).
evidence: Sequence analysis and comparison to known B56 substrate motifs cited (Hertz et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016b; Wang et al., 2016a; Wu et al., 2017a)

claim: The GST-tagged PME-1 B56 SLiM peptide (247–263) binds to B56γ1 with a binding affinity of ~13 μM measured by ITC.
source: The GST-tagged PME-1 B56 SLiM peptide (247–263) binds to B56γ1 with a binding affinity of ~13 μM measured by isothermal titration calorimetry (ITC).
evidence: Supported by ITC measurement data

claim: Full-length PME-1 interacts with B56γ1 with a binding affinity of 0.4 μM.
source: Full-length PME-1 (PME-1 FL) interacts with B56γ1 with a binding affinity of 0.4 μM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, left).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: Deletion of the internal loop harboring the B56-SLiM (ΔIL) abolishes PME-1 interaction with B56γ1 completely.
source: The deletion of the internal loop harboring the B56-SLiM (ΔIL) abolishes their interaction completely and deletion of N-terminal 18 residues (ΔN18) reduces the binding affinity by ~eightfold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, middle and right).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: Deletion of N-terminal 18 residues (ΔN18) reduces PME-1 binding affinity to B56γ1 by ~eightfold.
source: The deletion of the internal loop harboring the B56-SLiM (ΔIL) abolishes their interaction completely and deletion of N-terminal 18 residues (ΔN18) reduces the binding affinity by ~eightfold (Figure 2—figure supplement 1a, middle and right).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1a

claim: PME-1 binds directly to PR70 with a binding affinity of 0.7 μM.
source: PME-1 binds directly to PR70 with a binding affinity of 0.7 μM.
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: ΔIL reduces PME-1 binding affinity to PR70 by ~twofold.
source: ΔIL reduces the binding affinity by ~twofold, and ΔN18 completely abolishes this interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: ΔN18 completely abolishes PME-1 interaction with PR70.
source: ΔIL reduces the binding affinity by ~twofold, and ΔN18 completely abolishes this interaction (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by ITC data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: PME-1 interacts with Bα, which was weakened by ΔN18 but barely affected by ΔIL.
source: Using titration pulldown assay, we showed that PME-1 also interacts with Bα, which was weakened by ΔN18 but barely affected by ΔIL (Figure 2—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by pulldown assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1c

claim: The PME-1 internal loop harbors a primary B56-docking motif.
source: As summarized in Figure 2a, these data indicate that the PME-1 internal loop harbors a primary B56-docking motif, and the N-terminal disordered region possesses a Bα- and PR70-docking motif.
evidence: Inference from mapping data summarized in Figure 2a

claim: The N-terminal disordered region of PME-1 possesses a Bα- and PR70-docking motif.
source: As summarized in Figure 2a, these data indicate that the PME-1 internal loop harbors a primary B56-docking motif, and the N-terminal disordered region possesses a Bα- and PR70-docking motif.
evidence: Inference from mapping data summarized in Figure 2a

claim: ΔN18 decreased PME-1 interactions with all three PP2A holoenzymes (PP2A-B56γ1, PP2A-Bα, and PP2A-PR70).
source: ΔN18 decreased PME-1 interactions with all three PP2A holoenzymes (Figure 2b–d), consistent with the critical role of the N-terminal motif in binding to all three regulatory subunits (Figure 2a).

claim: ΔIL had a major effect on PME-1 interaction with the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme.
source: Similarly, ΔIL had a major effect on interaction with the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme (Figure 2b) but a minor effect on interactions with PP2A-Bα and PP2A-PR70 holoenzymes (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: Supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 2b

claim: ΔIL had a minor effect on PME-1 interactions with PP2A-Bα and PP2A-PR70 holoenzymes.
source: Similarly, ΔIL had a major effect on interaction with the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme (Figure 2b) but a minor effect on interactions with PP2A-Bα and PP2A-PR70 holoenzymes (Figure 2c, d).
evidence: Supported by gel filtration data shown in Figure 2c, d

claim: The interaction between the SYT16 peptide and PP2A-B56γ1 was blocked by increasing concentrations of PME-1.
source: By competition pulldown assay, we showed that the interaction between the SYT16 peptide and PP2A-B56γ1 was blocked by increasing concentrations of PME-1 (Figure 2e, left and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Supported by competition pulldown data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a

claim: No competitions were detected between PME-1 ΔIL or PME-1 ΔN18 and the PP2A-B56γ1 substrate peptide SYT16.
source: No competitions were detected between PME-1 ΔIL or PME-1 ΔN18 and this PP2A-B56γ1 substrate peptide (Figure 2e, left and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).
evidence: Supported by competition pulldown data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a

claim: Bα was recently reported to interact with CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 3 (CRTC3) and regulates CRTC3 phosphorylation and CREB transcriptional activity.
source: Bα was recently reported to interact with CREB-regulated transcription coactivator 3 (CRTC3) and regulates CRTC3 phosphorylation and CREB transcriptional activity (Sonntag et al., 2019).

claim: PME-1 competes with the CRTC3 motif for interaction with the PP2A-Bα holoenzyme.
source: PME-1 competes with this CRTC3 motif for interaction with the PP2A-Bα holoenzyme (Figure 2e, middle and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a).

claim: The PR70 regulatory subunit was previously shown to recognize a peptide motif in Cdc6 and control the cellular level of Cdc6 during cell cycle.
source: The PR70 regulatory subunit was previously shown to recognize a peptide motif in Cdc6 and control the cellular level of Cdc6 during cell cycle (Davis et al., 2008; Wlodarchak et al., 2013).

claim: PME-1 competes with Cdc6 for binding to the PP2A-PR70 holoenzyme.

claim: No competition was detected between PME-1 ΔN18 and the substrates of all three holoenzymes (PP2A-B56γ1, PP2A-Bα, and PP2A-PR70).

claim: PME-1 ΔIL completely lost the ability to block substrate recognition by the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme.

evidence: Supported by competition pulldown data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a

claim: PME-1 ΔIL retained the ability to block substrate recognition by the PP2A-Bα and PP2A-PR70 holoenzymes.
source: PME-1 ΔIL completely lost the ability to block substrate recognition by the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme, but not the PP2A-Bα and PP2A-PR70 holoenzymes (Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a), consistent with the critical role of this loop for interactions with PP2A-B56γ1, but not the other two holoenzymes.
evidence: Supported by competition pulldown data shown in Figure 2e and Figure 2—figure supplement 3a

claim: The presence of PME-1 blocked the binding of all peptide motifs recognized by the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme and reduced the counts for all B56-binding motifs to zero in phage selection.
source: The data showed that the presence of PME-1 blocked the binding of all peptide motifs recognized by the PP2A-B56γ1 holoenzyme and reduced the counts for all B56-binding motifs to zero in phage selection (Figure 2—figure supplement 3b).
evidence: Supported by ProP-PD data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3b

claim: PME-1 binding can block substrate recognition of holoenzymes from three families, likely by PME-1's substrate-mimicking holoenzyme-docking motifs.

claim: The structure of the PP2A-B56γ1–PME-1 complex was determined at an overall resolution of 3.4 Å.

claim: The PP2A-B56γ1–PME-1 complex adopts a pentagram architecture with a size of 100 × 100 × 90 Å.

claim: The structural shifts in the A-subunit result in a 12 Å shift in B56 that alleviates the steric hindrance for PME-1 binding.

claim: The methylated PP2Ac tail no longer occupies the A–B56 interface in the holoenzyme–PME-1 complex compared to the holoenzyme.

claim: PME-1 binding to the holoenzyme results in four coherent mechanisms that suppress the holoenzyme functions: demethylation, binding to the phosphatase active site, occupying the B56 protein groove for recruiting substrates, and perturbing the B56 internal loop.

claim: PME-1 undergoes a significant angular movement away from B56 up to 6 Å pivoted at the PME-1 helix that contacts the phosphatase active site.
source: PME-1 undergoes a significant angular movement away from B56 up to 6 Å pivoted at the PME-1 helix that contacts the phosphatase active site (Figure 3e).
